text: A Hadamard gate or a CNOT is a convenient abstraction. Underneath it, on real hardware, is nothing but a carefully shaped analog microwave or laser pulse. This lesson looks at what's inside that abstraction, and why some of the most important fidelity gains come from tuning the pulse itself.

When you write a circuit using a gate, a compiler eventually translates it into one or more physical control pulses. For a superconducting qubit, that's typically a microwave pulse at the qubit's resonant frequency, with some duration, amplitude, and phase. Amplitude controls how strongly the qubit is driven. Phase controls the axis of rotation on the qubit's state space. Frequency has to match the transition closely enough to drive it efficiently. And duration trades off against amplitude for a given rotation, while also interacting with error — longer pulses give decoherence more time to act. Every one of these parameters is calibrated per qubit, because no two physical qubits on a chip are identical.

Most users interact at the gate level: write a circuit out of a fixed library like X, H, CNOT, and the provider's compiler maps each to its own pre-calibrated default pulse — simpler, and the right level for most work. Some frameworks also expose pulse-level control, popularized under names like OpenPulse, letting an advanced user bypass the default gate definitions and specify the pulse shape directly, sample by sample. That's strictly more work and more fragile, but it opens optimizations gate-level programming can't reach, because the provider's default is tuned to be good on average, not optimal for your specific circuit or qubit.

A well-known example is the DRAG pulse, short for Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate, used on superconducting qubits. A simple pulse meant to drive a rotation can unintentionally leak some probability into a higher, unwanted energy level, because real superconducting qubits aren't perfect two-level systems. A DRAG pulse corrects for this by adding a small additional component derived from the pulse's own envelope that actively suppresses that leakage. The result is a gate that runs faster, or with lower error, than a naively-shaped pulse would allow at the same speed — a real, measurable gain from shaping the pulse, not from changing the hardware.
Next lesson: why a chip's error rates aren't a fixed spec printed on a datasheet — they're a snapshot of a system that keeps changing underneath you, and what providers do about it.
